chunks: And Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about interrupting the fast of expiation for an oath, expiation for zihar, and expiation for blood (diyah). He said: If upon a man is the fasting of two consecutive months, and he breaks his fast or falls ill in the first month, it is upon him to restart the fasting. And if he fasts the first month and fasts some part of the second month, then an excuse befalls him for which he has a valid reason, then it is only upon him to make up (the missed days). The approach in these narrations is to interpret them as: if his illness is one that does not prevent him from fasting, although it causes him some difficulty, then whenever the matter is as we mentioned, it becomes obligatory upon him to restart (the two months) according to what these narrations imply. And it is also possible to interpret them as a type of recommendation (istihbab) rather than obligation (fard) and necessity (ijab).

key_terms.الِاسْتِئْنَافُ: Restarting (the fast period from the beginning)
key_terms.كَفَّارَةِ الظِّهَارِ: Expiation for Zihar (a form of pre-Islamic divorce)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if one breaks the fast of expiation for two consecutive months due to illness?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from al-Sadiq (AS) to clarify the jurisprudential distinction between restarting the two-month expiation entirely versus merely making up missed days, depending on whether the illness prevents fasting or merely causes hardship. The text highlights the scholarly method of reconciling apparent contradictions by interpreting the ruling as either obligatory (wajib) or recommended (mustahabb) based on the specific nature of the impediment. This reflects the Shia emphasis on precise conditions for kaffarah, particularly regarding the continuity required for expiatory fasting.
